title: Savoring joy
hookLine: Thoreau sits in his sunny doorway from sunrise till noon and grows 'like corn in the night'
tomorrow: how did one monk know his friend's news before he heard it?

cards: A sunset gets photographed, and looked at later on a screen. Henry David Thoreau, living in his cabin by Walden Pond, did something else.

In Walden, he writes that on some summer mornings, after his bath, he sat in his sunny doorway from sunrise till noon, among the pines and hickories, in undisturbed solitude and stillness, while the birds sang around him or flitted through the house.
Hours. Doing, by most measures, nothing.

teach.b: Then comes the line that makes it a teaching: "I grew in those seasons like corn in the night."
He insists those hours weren't time taken out of his life; they were far better, he says, than any work of the hands would have been.

teach.h: A BROAD MARGIN TO MY LIFE.
teach.b: And from the same chapter: "I love a broad margin to my life." That's a Walden idea worth keeping: a good life needs margin, unfilled space around the work, the way a page needs white space around the words.
Savoring happens in the margin. You don't add more to a good moment.
You give it room. And look at his picture: Thoreau compared himself to corn, which does its growing in the dark, when nobody's watching. So savoring isn't a technique.
It's a margin, kept on purpose. That's this week, too.
It began in suffering: calling out, sitting in silence with someone, a hope with feathers, Jacob's beautiful patience, a wall rising stretch by stretch.
And it turned toward joy that's allowed. Savoring is how that joy gets to stay a little longer.

how: In Walden ('Sounds'), Thoreau describes whole mornings in his doorway and calls for 'a broad margin' to life. On a personal path, savoring means leaving unfilled time around a good moment so it can be felt.

o: eating very slowly so you notice every flavor
saving a good thing for later so it isn't used up
staying with a good moment and giving it room

games.q: this week's lines: tap the pairs.

s: Thoreau called his doorway mornings wasted time
he says he grew in those seasons like corn in the night.
Thoreau wrote, "I love a broad margin to my life"
in the chapter of Walden called 'Sounds'.
Jacob's beautiful patience meant hiding his grief
his eyes went white with sorrow; he took his complaint to God alone.

games.q: your friend's baby took her first steps at dinner. everyone grabs their phones to film the next try. what would Thoreau's margin suggest?
o: watch with your own eyes and let the moment take up the room.
film it all, so you can savor it properly later.
move on quickly, so the moment doesn't get overhyped.
games.why: Thoreau's savoring is a margin around the good moment: room to be in it, not to manage it.

practice: Close your eyes and bring back one good moment from this week; small is fine. Stay in it the way Thoreau stayed in his doorway: the light, the sound, who was there. Don't explain it to yourself; let it take up the whole margin.

wordCard.voice: Savoring joy: giving a good moment room to stay, the broad margin Thoreau loved.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: savor, and leave a broad margin around the good. That's the week, done.
